title: Physician Compensation Negotiation Guide (CleanClaimRx Operational Playbook Series; subtitle: Read the Contract. Know the Numbers. Negotiate from Strength.)
audience: Cover and preface: employed physicians, physicians evaluating an employment offer, and physicians renegotiating their compensation. A boilerplate disclaimer pasted into the Introduction instead describes the material as workflow content for billing teams.
summary: Consumer-style primer for a physician reading an employment offer. It covers base-salary benchmarking against MGMA percentiles, wRVU conversion factors and thresholds, collections-based pay, productivity, quality/access, signing and retention bonuses, malpractice tail and benefit valuation, non-compete and non-solicitation terms, first-year ramp-up cash planning, contract red flags, negotiation framing and a pre-signature checklist. Central method: translate each clause into dollars by projecting pay at 25th, 50th and 75th percentile production, test whether incentives are really attainable by asking for historical payout rates, price the cost of leaving (tail, restrictive covenant, bonus repayment), rank asks by negotiability, and have a healthcare employment attorney review before signing. It supplies no benchmark values, no state-specific law, no citations and nothing from the employer's side. For an owner-employer it is useful mainly in reverse: the questions a prepared hire, or the owner himself after a sale, will ask.

outline.gist: Names the audience, disclaims legal advice, and frames the content as vocabulary, benchmarks and analysis rather than demands.

outline.section: Introduction: The Agreement Is Already Written for Them
outline.gist: Employer-drafted agreements protect the employer; negotiating is normal. Promises income modeling skills. Ends with an unrelated billing-team and AI-draft disclaimer.
Benchmark base against MGMA percentiles, separate base from total pay, secure a guarantee period, and find clauses letting the employer cut the base.

outline.section: Section 2: The wRVU Model - Reading Your Productivity Threshold
outline.gist: Explains conversion factor and threshold, compares threshold with median production, projects pay at three production levels, and criticizes cliff bonuses.
Collections pay exposes the physician to payer mix and billing performance; wRVU pay insulates; collections favors physicians who control schedule and mix.
Productivity, quality/access, signing and retention bonuses; test attainability with cohort payout history; watch gross-repayment clauses; size bonuses in three scenarios.

outline.section: Section 5: Benefits, Tail Coverage, and the Hidden Economics
outline.gist: Claims-made versus occurrence malpractice cover, tail cost and who pays by termination type, and dollar valuation of health, retirement, CME and other benefits.
Radius, duration, multi-site zones, state-variable enforceability, litigation cost, carve-outs and buyout to negotiate, and limits on telling patients about departure.
Year-one production lags steady state; the guarantee bridges it; compute after-tax, after-loan cash margin; ramp-up length differs by specialty.

outline.section: Section 8: Red Flags in Employment Agreements
outline.gist: Seven warning patterns: unilateral modification, high thresholds, vague metrics, undefined non-compete, silent tail terms, overbroad non-solicitation, no dispute process.
Non-adversarial framing, a table ranking terms by negotiability, conversation before redline, one data-backed ask, attorney review before signing.

outline.section: Section 10: Before You Sign - The Pre-Signature Checklist
outline.gist: Twenty-seven confirmations across compensation, benefits and tail, non-compete and departure, term and governance, and final attorney review.

outline.section: Appendix: Glossary and Quick Reference Tables
outline.gist: Twelve-term glossary, a blank three-scenario income worksheet, and a six-question non-compete evaluation table.
Cross-sell page for three sibling playbooks: compensation design, Stark and Anti-Kickback awareness, and practice valuation.

framework_elements: Base salary benchmarking against survey percentiles
Payer-mix and billing-performance risk allocation in provider pay
Collection-rate transparency to providers (net versus gross)
Bonus attainability testing using historical payout rates
Quality and access incentive metric definition
Signing bonus repayment and vesting terms
Tail coverage responsibility by termination scenario
Non-compete radius, duration and site scope
Patient notification and continuity on provider departure
Compensation calculation audit right and dispute resolution
Term, renewal, notice and for-cause termination definitions
New-provider ramp-up and first-year cash planning
Negotiation prioritization by negotiability and dollar impact
Healthcare employment attorney review before signature

processes.name: Benchmark the offer's base and total compensation
steps: Obtain current survey percentiles for total compensation and wRVUs for the specialty and region
Place the base on that distribution and confirm whether bonus potential sits on top of it
Compare realistic total pay, not base alone, with the benchmark
Confirm the guarantee period length and request one if absent
Locate every clause that lets the employer lower the base (productivity shortfall, site volume, FMV determination, discretionary change)
processes.owner_role: Physician candidate (the document assigns every step to the physician; there is no employer-side owner)
processes.cadence: Once per offer or renegotiation, before signing

processes.name: Three-scenario wRVU income projection
steps: Collect expected annual wRVUs (own prior-year actuals or specialty median), the contract conversion factor and the threshold
Multiply wRVUs by the conversion factor at 25th, 50th and 75th percentile production
Take the greater of base and productivity pay in each scenario
Add conservative, median and strong estimates of quality or access bonus
Compare each scenario total with the matching survey total-compensation percentile
Identify whether the incentive is a cliff or a continuous per-wRVU rate
processes.cadence: Once per offer; rerun at renegotiation

processes.name: Productivity threshold and bonus attainability test
steps: Compare the contract threshold with median wRVU production for the specialty
Treat a threshold at or under the median as reasonable and one above the 75th percentile as a red flag
Ask HR or the recruiter how many physicians in the role earned the bonus in each of the last two to three years and what share of eligible pay it was
Leave out of income planning any bonus most of the cohort misses or that is discretionary
Require written metric definitions, measurement method, payment timing and dispute process
processes.owner_role: Physician candidate, with HR or recruiter supplying payout history

processes.name: Collections-based offer due diligence
steps: Request the practice-wide and panel-specific collection rate
Request payer mix by commercial, Medicare, Medicaid and self-pay
Establish who controls panel assignment and scheduling
Review the three-year billing and collections trend
Decide whether a collections or wRVU basis fits the control the physician will actually have
processes.owner_role: Physician candidate; practice supplies the data

processes.name: Malpractice tail and benefits valuation
steps: Identify whether coverage is claims-made or occurrence
Map who buys tail under resignation, termination without cause and termination for cause
Estimate tail cost for the specialty and market and spread it over expected tenure
Put a dollar value on health, retirement, CME, licensure, disability and loan-repayment benefits
Add benefit value to cash pay when comparing offers

processes.name: Restrictive covenant evaluation
steps: Record radius, duration and whether each practice site creates its own zone
Draw the restricted area on a map against home and alternative employers
Obtain a state-specific legal opinion on enforceability
Request carve-outs: hospital privileges, existing patients, termination without cause, and a pre-agreed buyout sum
Read the patient-notification and non-solicitation limits that apply on departure
processes.owner_role: Physician candidate with a healthcare employment attorney
processes.cadence: Before signing; revisit before any decision to leave

processes.name: First-year cash margin calculation
steps: Estimate year-one income from the guarantee or from ramp-up production times the conversion factor
Subtract federal tax, student-loan payments and fixed living costs
Treat a negative or thin remainder as grounds to negotiate a higher or longer guarantee
Confirm three to six months of reserves
Ask how long the last hire in the role took to reach benchmark production

processes.name: Negotiation conversation and pre-signature sign-off
steps: Rank desired changes by dollar impact and by how negotiable the term usually is
Ask for a call or meeting rather than opening with a marked-up contract
Present market data and one specific requested change with rationale
Ask which terms are fixed by group policy and which are flexible
Have a healthcare employment attorney licensed in the state review the final document
Confirm every verbal promise appears in writing and complete the 27-item checklist
processes.owner_role: Physician candidate; healthcare employment attorney for final review

metrics.name: Base salary percentile position
metrics.definition: Where the guaranteed base falls on the specialty compensation distribution
metrics.target: 50th percentile described as a market offer; above the 75th as a generous floor
metrics.red_flag: Base at the 25th percentile is called a low offer
metrics.source_cited: MGMA Physician Compensation and Production Report (named; no values given)

metrics.name: wRVU conversion factor
metrics.definition: Dollars paid per work RVU generated
metrics.formula: productivity pay / wRVUs (stated in the contract as dollars per wRVU)
metrics.target: National range roughly $45 to $65; primary care $58 called high end; surgical $62 called competitive
metrics.red_flag: Primary care $48 called below market median
metrics.source_cited: none (reader told to calibrate with current MGMA data)

metrics.name: Productivity-based compensation
metrics.definition: Pay generated by production under a wRVU model
metrics.formula: annual wRVUs x conversion factor (example 5,000 x $52 = $260,000)

metrics.name: Productivity threshold percentile
metrics.definition: wRVU level at which incentive pay starts, expressed against specialty production percentiles
metrics.target: At or below the MGMA 50th percentile wRVU figure
metrics.red_flag: At or above the 75th percentile (Section 2 says above; Section 8 says at or above)

metrics.name: Implied break-even production
metrics.definition: Production level at which productivity pay overtakes the base

metrics.name: Expected compensation by scenario
metrics.definition: Projected total pay in slow, typical and strong years
metrics.formula: max(base, wRVUs x conversion factor) + estimated quality or access bonus, at 25th, 50th and 75th percentile wRVUs
metrics.target: Compare each scenario with the matching MGMA total-compensation percentile
metrics.red_flag: Advertised total reachable only in the strong-year scenario

metrics.name: Net collection rate
metrics.definition: Share of allowed or collectible charges actually collected
metrics.target: 85% to 95% described as typical of a well-run practice

metrics.name: Gross collection rate
metrics.definition: Collections measured against billed charges before contractual adjustments
metrics.target: Commonly 50% to 80%; a low figure alone is said not to prove poor billing

metrics.name: Collections-based pay
metrics.definition: Physician pay as a fixed share of net collections attributed to the physician's encounters
metrics.formula: contract percentage x net collections (example 45% x $750,000 = $337,500)
metrics.red_flag: Assigned or Medicaid-heavy payer mix; inconsistent billing performance

metrics.name: Procedural collections rate for favoring a collections model
metrics.definition: Physician-level collections rate at which a collections formula may beat a wRVU formula

metrics.name: Bonus cohort payout rate
metrics.definition: Share of physicians in the same role who actually earned the productivity bonus in each recent year, and the bonus as a share of eligible pay
metrics.formula: physicians paid the bonus / physicians eligible, per year for the last two to three years
metrics.red_flag: A bonus about 80% of the cohort never earns is not plannable income

metrics.name: Quality and access bonus share
metrics.definition: Quality and access incentive relative to base pay
metrics.formula: quality and access bonus / base salary
metrics.red_flag: Metrics undefined, not measurable by the physician, or awarded at discretion

metrics.name: Baseline-scenario bonus value
metrics.definition: Dollar bonus expected at median production and median quality scores
metrics.target: $25,000 or more deserves weight in planning
metrics.red_flag: Under $10,000 is not a meaningful component; value only in the strong scenario is upside only

metrics.name: Signing bonus size and repayment window
metrics.definition: Lump sum at hire with a repayment duty if the physician leaves early
metrics.target: Typically $10,000 to $50,000; repayment window typically 12 to 36 months
metrics.red_flag: Repayment of the gross amount after tax was paid, with no gross-up

metrics.name: Tail coverage cost
metrics.definition: Price of extended reporting coverage after a claims-made policy ends
metrics.formula: annual premium x 1 to 3; for offer valuation divide by expected tenure
metrics.target: $8,000 to $20,000 primary care; $30,000 to $100,000 or more for surgery, OB/GYN, emergency medicine
metrics.red_flag: Contract silent on who pays in any termination scenario

metrics.name: Benefit value
metrics.definition: Cash-equivalent value of employer-paid benefits
metrics.formula: premium equivalent or face value per component, summed
metrics.target: Family health premiums $15,000 to $25,000 a year; CME, licensure, DEA, boards and dues $3,000 to $8,000 a year; packages can differ by $30,000 or more

metrics.name: Non-compete radius and duration
metrics.definition: Distance and time for which post-employment practice is barred
metrics.target: Common structures 10 to 25 miles and 12 to 24 months
metrics.red_flag: No defined radius or duration; every site creating its own zone

metrics.name: Guarantee period length
metrics.definition: Time during which the base is paid regardless of production
metrics.target: One year typical; 18 or 24 months for long ramp-up specialties
metrics.red_flag: No guarantee for a new hire in a new market or site

metrics.name: Year-one production ratio
metrics.definition: First-year wRVUs relative to eventual steady-state wRVUs
metrics.formula: year-one wRVUs / steady-state wRVUs (examples 2,500 of 4,500; 2,800 of 5,000 = 56%)

metrics.name: Ramp-up time to steady state
metrics.definition: Months for a new physician to reach the production the pay model assumes
metrics.target: Primary care 12 to 18 months; referral-dependent proceduralists 18 to 24 months; hospital-based roles faster
metrics.red_flag: Practice cannot or will not say how long the last hire took

metrics.name: First-year margin for error
metrics.definition: Cash left after tax, student loans and fixed living costs in year one
metrics.formula: year-one income - federal tax - student-loan payments - fixed living expenses
metrics.target: Positive with cushion; 3 to 6 months of reserves

numeric_claims.claim: National range for physician conversion factors is roughly $45 to $65 per wRVU, with specialty variation
Primary care conversion factor of $48 is below the market median, $58 is on the high end, a surgical $62 is competitive
wRVU-based pay is the model in most employed physician settings
MGMA report is published annually with compensation by specialty at the 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentiles
numeric_claims.source_cited: MGMA Physician Compensation and Production Report (named)

numeric_claims.claim: Base at the 25th percentile is a low offer, 50th is a market offer, above the 75th is a generous guaranteed floor
A one-year guarantee period is typical; some offers run 18 or 24 months
A physician who would produce 4,500 wRVUs in year two may produce 2,500 in year one
A threshold above the 75th percentile means the majority of physicians in similar roles will never earn the bonus
Well-run practices typically collect 85% to 95% of allowed or collectible charges (net collection rate)
Gross collection rate is commonly in the 50% to 80% range
At 45% of net collections, $750,000 collected pays $337,500 and $500,000 pays $225,000
Seeing 20 patients a day corresponds to about 4,800 wRVUs a year
Collections models can beat wRVU models for procedural physicians whose collections rate is consistently above 90%
Quality and access bonuses are often 5% to 15% of base compensation
Signing bonuses are typically $10,000 to $50,000 for employed physicians
Signing bonus repayment obligations typically run 12 to 36 months
A $30,000 signing bonus nets about $21,000 after tax, yet the $30,000 gross may be owed back on leaving in month 18
Retention bonuses are often paid at 12, 24 or 36 months
A baseline-scenario bonus under $10,000 is not meaningful for planning; $25,000 or more deserves weight
Benefit terms can make identical-salary packages differ by $30,000 or more
Tail coverage can cost one to three times the annual malpractice premium
Tail for surgery, OB/GYN and emergency medicine can be $30,000 to $100,000 or more
Tail for a primary care physician might be $8,000 to $20,000
Family health insurance premiums for a physician can run $15,000 to $25,000 a year
CME, licensure, DEA, board fees and dues often total $3,000 to $8,000 a year
Non-competes commonly use a 10 to 25 mile radius and a 12 to 24 month restriction
A physician headed for 5,000 wRVUs may produce 2,800 in year one and earn 56% of steady-state income without a guarantee
Primary care physicians in panel-building models may take 12 to 18 months to reach steady state
Referral-dependent proceduralists may face 18 to 24 month ramp-up in new markets
Three to six months of reserves are advised to bridge the first-year income gap

checkable_claims.claim: National range for physician conversion factors is roughly $45 to $65 per wRVU; a primary care conversion factor of $48 is below the market median, $58 is on the high end, and a surgical $62 is competitive.
checkable_claims.why: Anchors any wRVU rate the practice offers a hire and any judgment of a post-sale employment offer. The range is unsourced and looks several years stale; using it could underprice an offer or misjudge one. Check against current MGMA, AMGA and SullivanCotter pay-per-wRVU medians, including nurse practitioner figures the guide never gives.

checkable_claims.claim: FMV (Fair Market Value): the value in arm's-length transactions consistent with general market value - the standard used by Stark Law to evaluate physician compensation; MGMA benchmarks are used as the primary FMV reference.
checkable_claims.why: Medical-director stipends and any pay involving referral sources must be defensible as fair market value. Treating one survey as the FMV reference, or FMV as the only test, misreads 42 CFR 411.351 and CMS's refusal to adopt survey or percentile safe harbors, and ignores commercial reasonableness and the volume-or-value test.

checkable_claims.claim: The MGMA Physician Compensation and Production Report, published annually, shows compensation at the 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentiles; the MGMA benchmark figures represent total compensation - base salary plus all incentives and bonuses.
checkable_claims.why: If MGMA total compensation excludes employer-paid benefits while the guide's own glossary includes them, every benchmark comparison built on the guide is skewed. Also confirm the product's current name, cost of access and percentile set, since the look-it-up instruction assumes free availability.

checkable_claims.claim: Some states - California is the most notable example - largely do not enforce physician non-competes on public policy grounds. Other states enforce them strictly. Many states evaluate non-competes on a reasonableness standard.
checkable_claims.why: Florida enforces restrictive covenants under s. 542.335 with statutory presumptions and has a physician-specific rule in s. 542.336; the guide gives no state detail and omits the federal rule's rise and fall and the 2023-2025 state laws restricting physician non-competes. The owner needs the real rule to bind hires and to price his own post-sale covenant.

checkable_claims.claim: Courts in many states will interpret ambiguous non-compete terms against the employer who drafted them, but reaching that resolution requires litigation.
checkable_claims.why: Florida s. 542.335(1)(h) appears to bar courts from construing a restrictive covenant narrowly or against its drafter, the opposite of this advice. Relying on the guide would overstate a restricted clinician's leverage in Florida and understate an employer's.

checkable_claims.claim: Tail coverage can cost one to three times your annual malpractice premium. For high-risk specialties that can be $30,000 to $100,000 or more. For a primary care physician, it might be $8,000 to $20,000.
checkable_claims.why: Tail is a five-figure exit cost for the owner at sale or wind-down and for any departing clinician. The multiple and the primary-care dollar range are unsourced, and Florida premiums differ from national norms. Check carrier rate filings or broker quotes for family medicine and nurse practitioner cover in the practice's county.

checkable_claims.claim: Some agreements treat the signing bonus as taxable income at receipt but require repayment of the gross amount; you could pay taxes on $30,000, net $21,000, and then owe $30,000 back if you leave in month 18.
checkable_claims.why: An employer drafting a repayment clause must run payroll correctly. The guide omits how prior-year repayments work: gross repayment is the normal rule, the employer corrects FICA on Form 941-X, and the employee recovers income tax through the claim-of-right rule (IRC 1341). The stated loss may be overstated or misdescribed.

checkable_claims.claim: The practice collects typically 85% to 95% of allowed/collectible charges (the net collection rate) in a well-run practice; measured against billed charges (gross collection rate), the figure is commonly in the 50% to 80% range.
checkable_claims.why: Collections are the practice's core function. Calling 85% a well-run net collection rate conflicts with the usual 95%-plus target and would normalize large leakage on roughly $1 million of revenue. Listed because the number is unusual and probably conflicts with other titles in the same library.

adopt.idea: Run the guide backwards as an employer-side offer checklist: before any offer goes out, have a written answer for every question it trains candidates to ask (threshold versus median production, historical bonus payout, tail by termination scenario, modification rights, calculation audit and dispute process).
adopt.why: Informed candidates and their attorneys ask exactly these questions; unanswered ones stall recruiting or turn into disputes later.
adopt.note: Use for the current nurse practitioner agreement and any growth hire. Add NP-specific items the guide lacks: collaboration terms, split/shared and incident-to credit, payment at 85% of the physician fee schedule.

adopt.idea: Model every provider pay plan at low, expected and high production before adopting it, showing both provider pay and practice margin.
adopt.why: Shows whether advertised earnings are realistic and what the plan costs the practice when volume moves.
adopt.note: Use the practice's own AdvancedMD wRVU history by provider for the three scenarios instead of national percentiles, which describe differences between physicians, not one clinician's good and bad years.

adopt.idea: Pay incentives as a continuous or tiered per-wRVU rate rather than a single cliff bonus.
adopt.why: A cliff pays nothing at 98% of target and kills the incentive once the target is hit or out of reach.
adopt.note: Relevant when adding a productivity component to nurse practitioner pay.

adopt.idea: Choose the pay basis by who controls the risk: tie employed clinicians to wRVUs when the practice controls payer mix, assignment and billing; keep collections-based formulas for people who control those levers.
adopt.why: Keeps payer-mix and billing-performance risk with the party able to manage it and avoids disputes over collections the clinician cannot see.
adopt.note: Billing is in-house and payers are almost all government, so wRVU or encounter credit suits an employed NP; owner income stays a residual of collections. State in the contract which CMS fee-schedule year supplies the wRVU values.

adopt.idea: Write every quality or access incentive with an explicit metric definition, a data source the clinician can see, measurement period, payment date, and a calculation-audit and dispute step.
adopt.why: Discretionary or opaque bonuses do not motivate and are a common source of pay disputes.
adopt.note: Candidate metrics here: note-completion and charge-lag timeliness, annual wellness visit and advance care planning completion, chronic care management enrollment and monthly time capture.

adopt.idea: Track, and be ready to disclose, the share of clinicians who actually earned each incentive in prior years.
adopt.why: An incentive few people earn is a recruiting liability and a sign the threshold is mis-set.
adopt.note: Only two clinicians today; becomes useful when scaling and as a diagnostic in an advisory service for larger groups.

adopt.idea: Build a tail-coverage matrix: policy form, who pays tail under resignation, termination without cause and termination for cause, a current tail quote, and any tenure-based vesting.
adopt.why: Silence in the contract pushes the cost onto the clinician, and tail is a predictable five-figure exit cost.
adopt.note: Apply to the NP agreement and to the owner's own policy ahead of a sale or wind-down. Ask the broker about prior-acts (nose) coverage and free tail on death, disability or retirement, which the guide omits.

adopt.idea: Budget a ramp-up period for each new clinician and match any guarantee length to the realistic time to target production.
adopt.why: First-year production shortfalls are predictable and are a cash cost to whichever side carries the guarantee.
adopt.note: Facility census work ramps faster than an office panel; the real gating items here are payer enrollment and facility credentialing, which the guide never mentions.

adopt.idea: Treat restrictive covenants as a priced term: define radius from named sites, duration, carve-outs and a buyout amount at signing, and get state-specific counsel.
adopt.why: Vague covenants invite litigation; a pre-agreed buyout turns an injunction fight into a known number.
adopt.note: Florida law (ss. 542.335 and 542.336) should drive drafting; the same analysis applies to the covenant the owner would sign when selling the practice.

adopt.idea: Issue a total-rewards statement putting a dollar value on malpractice, tail accrual, health, retirement, CME, licensure and other benefits for each clinician.
adopt.why: Makes the full cost of each clinician visible for recruiting, retention and for normalizing provider cost in a valuation.
adopt.note: Feeds service-line profitability and sale-readiness work. Value employer retirement dollars and vesting directly rather than using the guide's match shortcut.

practice_relevance.why: Written for the employee across the table from the employer; the owner is the employer and has no offer to evaluate. Value is indirect: a mirror-image checklist for the nurse practitioner's agreement and future hires, a primer on the employment agreement the owner would be handed after selling to a health system or investor-backed group, and raw material for an advisory product. Nothing on nurse practitioner pay, split/shared or incident-to credit, facility-based rounding productivity, medical-director stipend valuation, independent-contractor arrangements or Florida law.
sections_that_do_not_apply: Section 1 and Section 2 benchmarking of the reader's own pay against physician survey percentiles (owner pay is a distribution and tax question, not a negotiated offer)
Section 3 as written for an employee choosing between pay bases (the practice sets the model and has almost no commercial payer mix)
Section 4 access bonuses (panel openness, appointment availability) and patient-satisfaction survey metrics (no office panel or front desk)
Section 4 signing and retention bonus advice from the recipient's side
Section 7 student-loan and household cash-flow planning
Section 7 office panel-building ramp-up timelines (facility census work ramps differently)
Section 9 scripts for dealing with recruiters and medical directors
Hospital-system framing throughout (uniform system pay models, HR, recruiters)

accuracy_concerns: Net collection rate of 85% to 95% is presented as typical of a well-run practice; the conventional target is 95% or better, so the stated floor would normalize roughly ten points of avoidable leakage. The 50% to 80% gross-rate range is arbitrary because gross rate depends on how high charges are set.

Conversion-factor range of $45 to $65 and the claim that $58 is high-end for primary care have no source and read like pre-2022 figures; recent survey medians for family and internal medicine pay per wRVU are, by analyst recollection, in the high $50s to low $60s (verify). No nurse practitioner rates at all.

FMV glossary entry tracks the Stark regulatory wording but calls MGMA the primary FMV reference. CMS has declined to treat any survey or percentile as a safe harbor, and FMV is one of three tests alongside the volume-or-value rule and commercial reasonableness.

The statement that courts often read ambiguous non-competes against the drafting employer is wrong for Florida: s. 542.335(1)(h) forbids construing a covenant narrowly or against the drafter, and (1)(g) bars weighing hardship to the restricted person (verify text).

Non-compete section names only California, whose ban is general rather than physician-specific, and gives no state rules. It is silent on state laws enacted 2023 to 2025 that ban or limit physician non-competes (for example Indiana, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Colorado, Texas; verify) and on the FTC rule issued in 2024, set aside, then abandoned in 2025.

Signing-bonus trap treats gross-versus-net repayment as only a drafting choice and omits the tax mechanics: prior-year repayments are normally gross, the employer corrects FICA, and the employee recovers income tax through IRC 1341 claim-of-right relief.

Glossary defines total compensation as including employer-paid benefits, while MGMA's total-compensation measure excludes benefit costs, so the instructed benchmark comparison can be apples to oranges.

Income worksheet uses max(base, wRVU x conversion factor), which fits only a greater-of model. It cannot represent a stated threshold, tiered rates, a cliff, a cap, or a draw with reconciliation, and it stands in national cross-sectional percentiles for one physician's good and bad years.

Says every employed physician has malpractice cover while employed and calls tail a separate policy. Florida allows physicians to meet financial-responsibility rules without insurance, tail is normally an extended-reporting endorsement, and prior-acts (nose) coverage is never mentioned.

Claims unilateral compensation-modification language is not standard; annual plan-amendment and FMV-adjustment clauses are common in health-system agreements, so the advice overstates negotiating room.

Benefit table values retirement as match percentage times the employee's contribution and ignores vesting schedules and the taxability of employer loan repayment and employer-paid disability benefits.
